title: Attribute
description: Understand named attribute roles, domains and values, and build explicit SQL projections without confusing labels with stored facts.
notes:
## An attribute names a property

An attribute is a named component of a relation schema, associated with a domain of permitted values. In Student(student_id, student_name, programme, score), score is an attribute; 86 is one possible value for that attribute in a particular tuple. The attribute supplies a role that remains understandable across many tuples, while its value can differ for each student.

The attribute is neither the whole relation nor one individual row. It helps describe what each tuple says. Naming attributes clearly makes the represented fact easier to read: student_id identifies a student, programme describes an academic affiliation, and score records a specified assessment measure. A collection of vague names such as value1 and value2 may be syntactically acceptable but leaves important meaning outside the schema.

## Names, domains, and values are different

The attribute name identifies a role. The domain describes the legal values for that role. The current value records the role's value in one tuple. For example, credits can be an attribute whose permitted values are whole numbers in a documented range. A particular course can have credits equal to four. Changing that course's credits changes data; changing the permitted range changes a validity rule.

An SQL type supplies part of a domain definition but may not capture all business meaning. INT permits many values inappropriate for course credits. A CHECK constraint can narrow a numeric range, while NOT NULL can make a value mandatory. Some rules depend on other attributes or referenced data and need additional enforcement. Do not equate a column's storage type with a complete account of valid business values.

## Similar types can describe different roles

Two attributes can share an integer representation while representing different concepts. student_id and advisor_id may both be integers, but one identifies the student described by the tuple and the other identifies an advisor. Matching storage types does not establish that the identifiers are interchangeable. The intended identity spaces and any foreign-key relationships still need definition.

Likewise, price and discount_amount can share a decimal type but describe different quantities. Even values with the same units may follow different validity rules. A price may be required to be positive while a discount may legitimately be zero. Treat shared representation as an implementation convenience, not proof that the attributes have identical semantics or should be merged into a single ambiguous column.

## Attribute names belong to a schema

Attribute names must distinguish roles within one relation schema. Different relations can reuse names such as id or name. Student.id and Course.id are therefore distinguishable when qualified by their relations. Reuse can be convenient, but a query combining relations must identify which role it means when a name would otherwise be ambiguous.

In SQL, table aliases provide shorter qualifiers, such as s.student_id. A qualifier does not change the student's identifier; it tells the query reader and engine where the referenced column comes from. Prefer explicit qualification in joins, especially when both sources contain similarly named columns. This reduces accidental connections based on a familiar label rather than the actual modeled relationship.

## Attribute count defines degree

The degree of a relation is its number of attributes. A Student schema with four attributes has degree four even when the relation is empty. Adding another student tuple changes cardinality, not degree. Adding a new attribute changes degree and introduces a new role that must be interpreted for existing and future tuples.

A SQL query can produce a different output degree from its source. SELECT student_id, programme returns two attributes even when the source table has four or more. Computed expressions can also introduce output attributes with explicit aliases. The source definition and the result definition are related, but they are not identical. Always read the selected output columns when interpreting a report's structure.

## Projection chooses the output roles

Projection retains specified attributes from input facts. In SQL, an explicit column list makes the output contract visible. SELECT * returns the available columns, which can change when the source schema changes. That is convenient during exploration but can create avoidable compatibility problems when an application expects a fixed result shape or positional mapping.

```sql
SELECT student_id, student_name AS display_name
FROM students
ORDER BY student_id;
```

Here display_name labels the result attribute derived from student_name. The alias does not rename the stored column or update any student name. The query still has one output row per source student unless other operations change that population. Keep output labeling separate from persistent schema changes and from modifications to actual data values.

## Renaming changes labels rather than facts

In relational algebra, rename can change relation or attribute labels while preserving the underlying value associations and tuple membership. This helps combine sources with overlapping names and makes derived results easier to reference. A proper rename does not change cardinality or convert every value to another domain simply because its displayed label changed.

SQL aliases are useful for query results, but persistent column renaming is a separate DDL operation. It can affect queries, generated types, application code, views, and other dependencies. Calling an output alias a database rename hides that difference. When documenting a query, say whether the label exists only in the result or whether an authorized schema migration would be required to change stored object names.

## Computed attributes need clear meaning

A result attribute can be calculated from stored values. For course work, a report might calculate total workload as lecture_hours plus lab_hours. Name the result total_hours and document the period being measured. A number without its meaning can be misused even when the arithmetic is correct. Two hours per week and two hours per semester are not equivalent facts.

Missing inputs require a deliberate policy. If lab_hours is NULL because the value is unknown, treating it as zero assumes something the database does not know. If the contract specifically defines NULL as no laboratory hours, COALESCE can implement that rule. The expression should follow the defined meaning of absence, rather than selecting a default solely to avoid a blank result.

## Attributes and keys serve related purposes

An attribute can participate in a key, but not every attribute is a key. student_name is a descriptive role and can repeat across students. A composite key can use more than one attribute, such as student_id together with course_id in a relation that permits one enrollment per pair. Uniqueness comes from the modeled rule and enforced constraints, not from the column name alone.

Attributes can also describe relationships. advisor_id is an attribute in Student even though its intended value points to an advisor fact elsewhere. A foreign key can enforce an appropriate reference. Merely ending a name with _id does not create that enforcement. Read constraints and relationships along with names when assessing the validity of a design or query.

## Reviewing attributes in practical work

For each attribute, ask what it means, which values it permits, whether absence is allowed, and whether its meaning depends on another role. Check that a selected alias describes the returned quantity accurately. Review repeated names across relations and qualify references where needed. Include repeated descriptive values and optional values in test data so that names are not accidentally treated as unique identifiers.

Document measurement scales and business ownership alongside the chosen labels. A useful attribute definition connects a stable name to a clear domain and purpose. That connection makes tuples readable and queries dependable. Explicit projection preserves the intended output contract, while careful aliases help readers interpret derived results. Separating names, values, types, and constraints prepares you to reason about domains, keys, schema evolution, and query composition without treating every column label as a complete specification.

questions.question_text: What is an attribute in the relational model?
options: A single row of data
A named column of a relation schema, bound to a domain of legal values
The total number of rows in a relation
A synonym for 'relation'
questions.explanation: An attribute is a named property/column of the schema, not a data value or a row.

questions.question_text: How many attributes does Students(id, name, department, gpa) have?
options: It depends on the number of rows
questions.explanation: There are four named columns: id, name, department, gpa.

questions.question_text: In the tuple (3, Meera, CS, 9.1), what role does 'gpa' play with respect to the value 9.1?
options: 'gpa' is the tuple and 9.1 is the attribute
'gpa' is the attribute name that holds the value 9.1 in this tuple
'gpa' and 9.1 are both attributes
'gpa' is a domain and 9.1 is a relation
questions.explanation: The attribute 'gpa' is the label; 9.1 is the actual value that attribute takes in this particular tuple.

questions.question_text: Which best distinguishes an Attribute from a Domain?
options: An attribute is the named role/column; a domain is the pool of legal values it may take
A domain is the row; an attribute is the table
They are identical concepts with different names
An attribute always has a larger set of values than its domain
questions.explanation: The attribute names a column; the domain defines what values are legally allowed for that column.

questions.question_text: Can two distinct attributes in different relations share the exact same name, such as 'id' in both Students and Courses?
options: No, attribute names must be globally unique across the entire database
Yes, attribute names only need to be unique within a single relation schema
No, this would violate domain integrity
Yes, but only if both relations have the same degree
questions.explanation: Uniqueness of attribute names is required only within one relation schema, not across the whole database.

questions.question_text: If 'id' (student id) and 'advisor_id' both draw from the integer domain, what does this illustrate?
options: Two attributes can share a domain while remaining distinct, differently-named attributes
They must actually be the same attribute
This is disallowed in the relational model
Domains can only be used by one attribute at a time
questions.explanation: Multiple attributes may be defined over the same domain (e.g., integer IDs) yet represent different, independently named roles.

questions.question_text: Renaming an attribute using the relational-algebra rename operator affects:
options: Only the schema's labeling; the underlying values in tuples are unchanged
The actual stored data values
The domain's set of legal values
The cardinality of the relation
questions.explanation: Rename is a purely structural/labeling operation; it does not alter any stored values.

questions.question_text: Why is 'gpa' considered an attribute rather than a value?
options: Because it appears in every tuple as the same fixed column label bound to a domain, not as a data item itself
Because it is numeric
Because it changes with every INSERT
Because it uniquely identifies each tuple
questions.explanation: 'gpa' is the constant column name across all tuples; the values it holds (like 9.1) vary per tuple, but the attribute name/role does not.

questions.question_text: Student has five attributes and no rows. What is its degree?
options: Zero
Five
One
Undefined
questions.explanation: Degree counts named attributes even in an empty relation.

questions.question_text: In credits = 4, which part is the attribute value?
options: credits
The whole schema
The table name
questions.explanation: The name supplies the role; four is the value in one tuple.

questions.question_text: What does student_name AS display_name change in a SELECT result?
options: The stored column name
Every stored name value
The output label
The source key constraint
questions.explanation: An alias labels the result without a persistent schema change.

questions.question_text: Why might SELECT * be unsuitable for a fixed application result contract?
options: It always deletes rows
It excludes identifiers
It automatically removes duplicates
New source columns can change its output shape
questions.explanation: An explicit projection states the expected output columns.

questions.question_text: Two relations each have an id column. How can a join identify the intended source?
options: Qualify the reference with a table name or alias
Delete one column first
Depend on physical column order
Assume both identifiers mean the same thing
questions.explanation: Qualification resolves which source attribute is referenced.

questions.question_text: Does an INT type completely define valid course credits?
options: Yes; every integer is valid credit
No; business restrictions can require further constraints
Yes; INT makes the column a key
No; integer values cannot be stored
questions.explanation: Representation and the complete domain rule are different.

questions.question_text: Why need price and discount_amount not share all validity rules?
options: Decimal attributes cannot coexist
Names automatically enforce their ranges
Their roles differ despite similar representations
Every price must equal its discount
questions.explanation: Distinct meanings can require different domain restrictions.

questions.question_text: What does SELECT student_id, programme determine about output degree?
options: It equals the source cardinality
It always equals the source degree
It is one because programme repeats
There are two selected attributes
questions.explanation: Output degree follows the result attribute list.

questions.question_text: Does naming a column advisor_id create a foreign key?
options: No; a reference constraint must actually be defined
Yes; the suffix is enforced
Only if it is last in the schema
Only if the table has rows
questions.explanation: A name communicates intent but does not implement reference integrity.

questions.question_text: When is replacing NULL lab_hours with zero justified?
options: Whenever a report looks cleaner
When the documented contract gives absence that meaning
Whenever the source is empty
When the column name is short
questions.explanation: Defaulting must preserve the intended meaning of missing information.

questions.question_text: Which statement about keys is accurate?
options: Every attribute is a key
Only name attributes can be keys
A key can consist of multiple attributes
A key is a displayed row number
questions.explanation: Composite keys use several attributes to identify a tuple.

questions.question_text: What does relational-algebra attribute renaming preserve?
options: Only disk page numbers
A new column value for every tuple
A different domain by definition
Tuple membership and underlying values
questions.explanation: Renaming labels does not inherently change facts or cardinality.

coding_problems.title: Project course identities and labels
coding_problems.task: Return course_id and course_name labeled display_name. Preserve repeated names; do not alter stored column names.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE courses (course_id INT PRIMARY KEY, course_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, lecture_hours INT NOT NULL, lab_hours INT NULL);
constraints: course_id is unique; hours are nonnegative supplied integers.
For the workload exercise only, NULL lab_hours is explicitly defined as no laboratory hours.
edge_cases: Zero laboratory hours and contract-defined absence must both work.
hints: Use AS for result labels and COALESCE only under the stated absence contract.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT course_id, course_name AS display_name FROM courses ORDER BY course_id;
coding_problems.explanation: Explicit projection and aliases specify the output attribute roles while preserving separate course identities.

coding_problems.title: Calculate a clearly named workload attribute
coding_problems.task: In this exercise NULL lab_hours means no laboratory hours. Return course_id and total_hours = lecture_hours plus laboratory hours for courses with at least four total hours. Sort by identifier.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE courses (course_id INT PRIMARY KEY, course_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, lecture_hours INT NOT NULL, lab_hours INT NULL);
constraints: course_id is unique; hours are nonnegative supplied integers.
For the workload exercise only, NULL lab_hours is explicitly defined as no laboratory hours.
edge_cases: Zero laboratory hours and contract-defined absence must both work.
hints: Use AS for result labels and COALESCE only under the stated absence contract.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT course_id, lecture_hours + COALESCE(lab_hours, 0) AS total_hours FROM courses WHERE lecture_hours + COALESCE(lab_hours, 0) >= 4 ORDER BY course_id;
coding_problems.explanation: Explicit projection and aliases specify the output attribute roles while preserving separate course identities.
